value.overview: The Black Hawk-Eagle (Spizaetus tyrannus) is a powerful forest raptor of the tropical Americas. It is named for its mostly black plumage, conspicuous crest, and bold white markings on the wings and tail. This eagle usually hunts from within or above forest, and its loud whistles may reveal its presence before the bird is seen. It is more tolerant of disturbed woodland than some related hawk-eagles, but still depends on mature trees and connected forest for nesting and hunting.
value.classification: The Black Hawk-Eagle belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. It is one of the forest-dwelling hawk-eagles in the genus Spizaetus.
value.identification: Adults are mostly black, with a short, bushy crest, yellow eyes and legs, and broad white checkering visible beneath the wings. The black tail has several broad whitish bands. In flight, the species has broad wings and a relatively long tail. Immatures are browner and show much more white on the head, throat, and underparts, with dark streaking or barring. Its far-carrying, whistled calls are often easier to detect than its quiet movements through the forest.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico through Central America and much of northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident, occurring mainly in humid lowlands and foothills on both the Caribbean slope and the southern Pacific slope. It is most frequent around roughly 200 to 1,000 meters but can occur to about 2,000 meters. Habitats include mature rainforest, forest edges, fragmented woodland, secondary growth, and partly open areas with tall trees. It is recorded in places such as La Selva, Braulio Carrillo, and southern Pacific forests.
value.migrationStatus: The Black Hawk-Eagle is considered resident in Costa Rica. It does not undertake a regular long-distance migration there, although individuals may move locally in response to food availability, weather, or changing habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but the species builds a large stick nest high in a tall emergent tree, often on a forested slope or near forest edge. A nest observed in Costa Rica was about 20 meters above the ground, and a chick has been documented near a nest in Guanacaste. Hawk-eagles generally lay a single egg, and the young depend on the adults for an extended period. Pairs are territorial and may remain associated with the same forest area year-round.
value.dietFeeding: The Black Hawk-Eagle takes a varied prey of medium-sized forest animals. Its diet includes mammals such as squirrels, rodents, opossums, and occasionally monkeys, as well as birds, bats, snakes, and large lizards. It commonly watches from a concealed perch or circles above the canopy before making a fast attack. In Costa Rica, its hunting grounds include forest interiors, edges, and partially open woodland where prey can be detected and pursued.
value.behavior: This eagle is usually solitary or seen in pairs. It often soars during the mid to late morning, using rising air currents above forested hills, but it may remain difficult to observe because it spends much time perched inside the canopy. Loud, clear whistles are frequently given in flight or near a territory. Adults defend breeding areas and use their strong talons to carry prey back to a nest or secluded feeding site.

conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing globally, although the Black Hawk-Eagle remains widespread and locally common or relatively common in suitable habitat. In Costa Rica it is more adaptable to habitat disturbance than some other forest hawk-eagles, but local abundance can still decline when mature forest is lost.
conservation.threats: The main concern is the continuing loss, fragmentation, and degradation of tropical forest, including the removal of large nesting trees. Expansion of agriculture, roads, settlements, and other development can reduce hunting habitat and isolate breeding territories. Disturbance near nests and illegal capture or killing may also affect local populations.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore mature forest, forest edges, and ecological connections between protected areas, especially in Costa Rica's Caribbean foothills and southern Pacific lowlands. Retain large emergent trees and avoid disturbance near active nests. Support protected areas, responsible land-use planning, and citizen-science monitoring. Do not capture, handle, or persecute wild raptors, and report suspected wildlife trafficking to the appropriate Costa Rican authorities.
